```{r}
#| label: preparo
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# The numbers on this page come from resultados/padaria.rds (Portuguese
# version of the case), written by scripts/indicadores.R.
caso <- "../../../projetos/mentoria-padaria"
source(file.path(caso, "scripts/rotulos.R"))
source(file.path(caso, "scripts/apresentacao.R"))
res <- ler_padaria(caso, "en")
tx <- res$tx
num <- tx$num; pct <- tx$pct; reais <- tx$reais
taxa <- function(p, f) res$sobra$taxa[res$sobra$produto == p & res$sobra$fornada == f]
mg <- function(p, coluna) res$margem[[coluna]][res$margem$produto == p]
salvar_capa(res, "img/capa.png", logo = file.path(caso, "../../assets/img/logo-branco.png"))
```

::: aviso-dados
**Sample mentoring material with fictional data.** Padaria Grão Dourado does not exist. The numbers were generated by a script, with known patterns, for the exercise.

[Download the template spreadsheet (.xlsx)](../../../projetos/mentoria-padaria/resultados/template_bakery.xlsx){download="template_bakery.xlsx"}
:::

## The exercise

In the group mentoring, from the second to the fifth session, each participant follows the same path with their own company's data: organize the spreadsheet, build the KPIs, read the numbers and decide. This page walks through that path with an example.

The owner of Grão Dourado has logged production and sales in a spreadsheet for years. The bakery is always busy, but profit doesn't keep up, and every evening there is bread left on the counter. Her question is simple: where is the money that doesn't show up?

## The spreadsheet as it is

`r num(res$dias)` days, from March 2 to May 24, 2026, one sheet per month. The first rows of March:

```{r}
#| label: baguncada
tabela_baguncada(res) |> kable(align = "l")
```

[The original spreadsheet is in Portuguese.]{.nota-idioma}

What gets in the way of any calculation:

- the date appears only once, merged over the day's rows, and in different formats ("02/03", "2026-03-03", "4 mar");
- the same product spelled several ways ("Pão francês", "Pao Frances", "francês"), and the same goes for batches ("6h", "06:00", "6 h");
- price and cost sometimes as numbers, sometimes as text with "R$";
- a weekly total row in the middle of the table;
- in April, the columns come in a different order.

## Organizing

The organized spreadsheet has one row per day, product and batch, always with the same columns: date, weekday, batch (6 a.m., 10 a.m., 2 p.m. or 5 p.m.), product, how many were baked, how many were sold, and the price and cost of one unit. That's `r num(res$linhas)` rows.

The cost is ingredients and packaging. Rent, wages and energy are left out, because they don't change with one batch more or less.

## The three numbers

### 1. Leftover rate by batch and product

Leftovers are what was baked and not sold. Divided by what was baked, they show where too much bread is being made.

::: so-computador
```{r}
#| label: sobra
#| fig-cap: "Leftover rate by product and batch over the 12 weeks: leftovers ÷ baked. The darker, the more is left over. Blank: a batch in which the product is not baked."
#| fig-alt: "Grid with the six products in rows and the four batches in columns. French rolls have few leftovers in the morning and many in the 5 p.m. batch. Cream donuts have about half left over in both batches. Cheese bread has almost none."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| lightbox:
#|   group: computador
grafico_sobra(res)
```
:::

::: so-celular
```{r}
#| label: sobra-celular
#| fig-cap: "Leftover rate by product and batch over the 12 weeks: leftovers ÷ baked. The darker, the more is left over. Blank: a batch in which the product is not baked."
#| fig-alt: "Grid with the six products in rows and the four batches in columns. French rolls have few leftovers in the morning and many in the 5 p.m. batch. Cream donuts have about half left over in both batches. Cheese bread has almost none."
#| fig-width: 4.8
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| lightbox:
#|   group: celular
grafico_sobra(res, celular = TRUE)
```
:::

French rolls have `r pct(taxa("frances", "6h"))` left over from the 6 a.m. batch and `r pct(taxa("frances", "17h"))` from the 5 p.m. batch: of the roughly `r num(res$fr17$produzido_dia)` rolls baked at 5 p.m., only `r num(res$fr17$vendido_dia)` sell each day. Cream donuts have about half left over in both batches. Cheese bread, on the other hand, sells almost everything: `r pct(100 - res$queijo$taxa, 1)` of what is baked.

### 2. Real margin by product

The owner's math was price minus cost for each unit sold. The real margin also subtracts the cost of what was left over: revenue minus the cost of everything baked.

::: so-computador
```{r}
#| label: margem
#| fig-cap: "Apparent margin (price minus cost for sold units only) and real margin (revenue minus the cost of everything baked), by product, over the 12 weeks."
#| fig-alt: "Paired bars by product. For almost all products, the real margin is a little below the apparent one. For cream donuts, the apparent margin is over 12 thousand reais and the real one is about 1.6 thousand."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| lightbox:
#|   group: computador
grafico_margem(res)
```
:::

::: so-celular
```{r}
#| label: margem-celular
#| fig-cap: "Apparent margin (price minus cost for sold units only) and real margin (revenue minus the cost of everything baked), by product, over the 12 weeks."
#| fig-alt: "Paired bars by product. For almost all products, the real margin is a little below the apparent one. For cream donuts, the apparent margin is over 12 thousand reais and the real one is about 1.6 thousand."
#| fig-width: 4.8
#| fig-height: 5
#| lightbox:
#|   group: celular
grafico_margem(res, celular = TRUE)
```
:::

By the old math, cream donuts brought in `r reais(mg("sonho", "margem_aparente"))` over 12 weeks. After leftovers, they bring in `r reais(mg("sonho", "margem"))`: almost everything they earn goes into what stays on the counter.

### 3. Share of total margin

Added up, the real margins come to `r reais(res$lucro_total)` over 12 weeks. That is what the bakery pays rent, wages and energy out of. How much comes from each product:

::: so-computador
```{r}
#| label: participacao
#| fig-cap: "Each product's share of total margin over the 12 weeks (sum of real margins, before rent, wages and energy)."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars. Cheese bread has the largest share of total margin, followed by baked savories and French rolls. Cream donuts have less than 1%."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| lightbox:
#|   group: computador
grafico_participacao(res)
```
:::

::: so-celular
```{r}
#| label: participacao-celular
#| fig-cap: "Each product's share of total margin over the 12 weeks (sum of real margins, before rent, wages and energy)."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars. Cheese bread has the largest share of total margin, followed by baked savories and French rolls. Cream donuts have less than 1%."
#| fig-width: 4.8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| lightbox:
#|   group: celular
grafico_participacao(res, celular = TRUE)
```
:::

Cheese bread, which sells out, accounts for `r pct(mg("queijo", "participacao"), 1)` of total margin, more than French rolls, which take up far more oven time. Cream donuts, which the owner saw as a best seller, account for `r pct(mg("sonho", "participacao"), 1)`.

## The decision

All three numbers point to the same place: the 5 p.m. oven is baking French rolls that don't sell, while cheese bread runs out. The decision in the exercise is to cut the 5 p.m. French roll batch in half, from about `r num(res$fr17$produzido_dia)` to `r num(res$fr17$produzido_dia / 2)` rolls, and use that oven for a batch of `r num(res$queijo$lote)` cheese breads.

The cut has a cost, and it goes into the math: on `r num(res$fr17$dias_falta)` of the `r num(res$dias)` days, demand at 5 p.m. was more than half the batch, so the bakery would miss about `r num(res$fr17$perdido_dia)` sales a day. Even so, the savings on what is no longer left over outweigh that loss.

For the new cheese bread batch, the math uses a range: demand is lower in the afternoon than in the morning, so the estimate goes from selling half to selling 80% of that batch.

::: destaque-suave
**Estimated savings: `r reais(res$faixa[["baixa"]])` to `r reais(res$faixa[["alta"]])` a month.** The numbers vary from business to business: what matters here is the method, not the amount.
:::

Before changing the routine, the owner tests it for two weeks and tracks the same three numbers in the spreadsheet.

## Do it with your numbers

The template spreadsheet has the entries sheet already organized, with Grão Dourado's 12 weeks as an example, and a KPIs sheet with the three numbers calculated by simple formulas. Delete the sample rows and enter your own: the KPIs update on their own. Works in Excel and Google Sheets.
